sections.h2: Where to search Escambia County records
sections.html:
Deeds and other recorded land documents live on the Clerk's Landmark Web official records site. Tax and value data sit on the Property Appraiser and Tax Collector sites. Landmark Web searches by name, document, case number, book and page, consideration, record date, clerk file number and legal description.

The appraiser's site, escpa.org, covers parcels in Escambia County, the City of Pensacola and the Town of Century, with values from the 2026 certified roll. The Tax Collector's site finds a tax account by name, address or account number. Parcel data on the appraiser's site is not survey quality, so hire a surveyor when boundaries matter.

sections.h2: Older records at the Clerk's Public Records Center
sections.html:
The Clerk's Public Records Center holds court, board and marriage records, along with historical files that can only be viewed in person. They come in handy for old titles and family land.

  • Circuit civil files from 1820 to 1985
  • The Government Survey of 1827
  • Marriage books from 1822 to 1999
  • Old wills and will books from the 1800s
  • Probate cases from 1883 to 1997
  • The Spanish Census of Pensacola, 1820

Online court records require registration, and the Clerk's page links to a registration agreement form and a search guide. Mortgage foreclosure sales in Escambia County are listed on the Clerk's Online Public Records page.

Florida sets recording charges by statute in section 28.24, and the Pensacola clerk follows that same schedule. Expect $5.00 on the opening page, $4.00 on each later page, and $1.00 for every name past the fourth.

Clerk recording charges, Florida Statutes s. 28.24(13)
ChargeAmount
First page$5.00
Each added page$4.00
Each name beyond four$1.00
Records modernization fund, first page$1.00
Records modernization fund, each added page$0.50
Added technology charge$4 per page

Your document's page count and the names on it move the total, so phone the Clerk for the figure that applies to your deed. The stamp tax is paid at that same window.

sections.h2: Check the record before you list
sections.html:
Before you list, pull the vesting deed and anything else recorded in your name. Landmark Web will let you retrace how title reached you by name, book and page, record date or legal description.

  • Compare the legal description on your last deed with the one attached to the tax account at the appraiser.
  • Look for recorded mortgages, liens or court documents that a payoff must clear.
  • Make sure each owner's name is spelled the same way on every instrument.
  • Note whether the parcel is inside Pensacola, Century or the unincorporated county, since that changes which non-ad valorem charges show on the tax bill.

A title agent repeats this search later. If something is off, you want to learn it now, while a fix will not collide with a buyer's deadline.

sections.h2: Documentary stamp tax on a deed
sections.html:
Escambia pays the usual Florida rate: 70 cents for each $100 of the sale price. Miami-Dade is the only county that pays less.

The amount taxed counts cash, a debt that gets wiped out and any mortgage on the land, even one the buyer does not assume. Whoever agreed to cover the tax, every party to the deed stays liable, and the clerk takes payment when the deed goes on record. Mortgages and notes are taxed at 35 cents per $100 secured. A note tops out at $2,450, while a mortgage has no ceiling.

  • Taxable: warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's and life estate deeds.
  • Also taxable: a deed in lieu of foreclosure and an agreement for deed.
  • Not taxable: a personal representative's deed under a probated will.
  • Exempt: a spousal homestead deed where the only consideration is a mortgage, and a divorce deed for the marital home.

Land can only be conveyed by a written deed with two witnesses watching the signing. Section 689.01 asks for two subscribing witnesses, drops the old seal requirement and permits witnessing over audio-video technology.

Before the paper goes to the Clerk, sit down with your title agent and check four things:

  • The legal description copies the prior recorded deed exactly.
  • Every owner of record signs, each in front of two witnesses.
  • Stamp tax is figured on the correct price.
  • A lawyer has looked at any lady bird deed. In one Department of Revenue advisement such a deed passed no present beneficial interest and owed no stamp tax on those facts, though different facts can change the answer.

sections.h2: Protecting a property from fake deeds
sections.html:
The Clerk's Landmark Web site offers Property Fraud Alert. Enroll a name, and you get an email every time a land records document is filed under it.

The service is free. It only reports recorded instruments and does not stop fraud. Still, an alert on your own name, and on the name of a deceased relative if you inherited the house, gives early warning of a forged deed. If an owner of family property has died and records were never updated, probate or another process may be needed to settle who owns it.

Three offices, three sets of files. Tax history is at the Tax Collector, and an unpaid bill goes delinquent April 1, after which a tax certificate can be issued. Foreclosure sales run through the Clerk. State law has the clerk schedule a foreclosure sale from 20 to 35 days after final judgment, and the top bidder leaves a 5 percent deposit.

For a house with probate history, ask the Public Records Center, which holds probate cases back to 1883 for in-person viewing. A shortened estate procedure called summary administration is open when the non-exempt estate is $150,000 or less, or when the decedent died more than two years before.

sections.h2: Marriage records, name changes and closing day
sections.html:
These records help when a signer's name changed or an heir must be proved. Marriage records from 1996 to the present are in the Public Records Center, and older books run back to 1822.

  • Marriage books: 1822 to 1999, viewed in person.
  • Microfiche: 1919 through 1995, plus indexes covering 1821 to 1900 and 1901 to 1918.
  • Records from 1996 forward: available through the Clerk's records service.

If your name differs between the vesting deed and your current ID, collect the marriage or court record that links the two names before you list. Otherwise the buyer's title company may stall the closing.

On closing day, bring photo ID and expect to sign the deed in front of the required witnesses. The title agent sends the signed deed to the Clerk for recording, and the stamp tax goes in with it. Afterward, ask the title agent for the recorded copy and file it with your closing papers. Its recording date and book and page numbers are what any later search will point to.

faqs.q: Where are Escambia County deeds recorded?
faqs.a: At the Clerk and Comptroller's office. The Landmark Web site lets you look up recorded papers by name, book and page, record date and several other fields.

faqs.q: What is the stamp tax on a deed in Escambia County?
faqs.a: The statewide rate of 70 cents per $100 of price. Everyone named on the deed is liable, and the clerk collects when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: How much is the first page recording fee in Florida?
faqs.a: $5.00 under section 28.24, plus $1.00 for the modernization fund and an added $4 per page technology charge. Each added page is $4.00 plus further charges.

faqs.q: Can I view Escambia County probate files from the 1800s online?
faqs.a: No. Old wills, probate cases from 1883 to 1997 and civil files from 1820 to 1985 can only be viewed at the Public Records Center.

faqs.q: Does Escambia County offer an alert for fraudulent deeds?
faqs.a: Yes. Enroll a name in the Clerk's free Property Fraud Alert and you are emailed whenever a document is filed under it. It reports fraud after the fact and cannot block it.
